newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds end stronger on gain from EMU.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds end stronger on gain from EMU.

text.p: Canadian bonds ended stronger on Wednesday in concert with rising U.S. bonds, which gained on a flight to quality from Europe.

Dealers said North American bonds rose on rumors of problems with the timetable for the European Monetary Union and in spite of calming comments from German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.18 to 111.15 to yield 7.059 percent for a spread of 23 basis points over the U.S. 30-year benchmark, which rose 17/32 to 97.14-15/32 to yield 6.83 percent.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima on Wednesday reaffirmed the commitment of each of their countries to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
Waigel told reporters after the meeting in Bonn that the timetable was not as important fulfiling the fiscal goals, while Klima said the treaty left room for interpretation.

Traders said the comments did little to calm the nervousness over the EMU timetable that has been sending the U.S. dollar into orbit and prompting fixed income investors to consider increasing their North American investments.
"There is clearly a preference to own currencies where growth prospects are strong and to move away from currencies where growth prospects are pretty bleak," said Michael Rosenberg at Merrill Lynch.
Traders said 10-year benchmark bond was up C$0.17 to 104.10 to yield 6.424 percent for a spread of 20 basis points below the U.S. 10-year benchmark.
While Europeans struggled with the EMU debate U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan said at his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony this week that the U.S. economy was doing "exceptionally well."
